annotations.text:
THE ACTUAL PROBLEM
It isn't that you use gold — it's that gold does every job: eyebrow, headline accent, button fill, links, rules, icons. Tiger Boards does exactly the same thing, which is why you collide.

Your logo spends gold in ONE place: a single dot marking a point on an arc — a checkpoint reached. That's a product metaphor, not a luxury one. Demote gold back to a point and the resemblance collapses while the logo still fits.

Row 1 keeps your logo. Row 2 (A/B/C) was drafted before I knew the logo was fixed — each replaces gold with another accent, so each fights the gold dot. Kept for reference, not recommended.

D · SWISS GRID — my pick
Your own cream and near-black, hard 12-column grid, 2px rules, Public Sans, flush left. No letterspaced gold eyebrow, no italic accent phrase.

The move: gold becomes one LARGE flat field, not a thin accent. Same pigment, opposite read — confident and institutional instead of luxury.

Why: biggest break per unit of effort, and it ships through the tokens you already have.
Tradeoff: stark. Needs real copy discipline — weak writing has nowhere to hide on a grid this bare.

E · BLUEPRINT
Drafting paper, fine grid, dimension lines, orthographic flow, IBM Plex Sans/Mono. Gold survives exactly as the logo uses it: the node dot marking each stage.

Why: the most on-message of the six — an ISMS IS a system you had built, and this is its drawing. Nobody in the space looks like this.
Tradeoff: the most bespoke work. Schematics have to be drawn per page, and a weak one looks worse than no diagram.

F · ALMANAC — lowest risk
Keeps cream, near-black and gold exactly where they are. Changes only the typographic voice: Instrument Serif (high contrast, editorial) replaces Fraunces, over your existing Manrope. Double rules, standing sidebar, drop cap.

Why: most of the sameness is the typeface. Swap the voice, keep every other piece of brand equity.
Tradeoff: still a serif on cream — the family resemblance to the genre is reduced, not severed.
